speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling has just provided an overview of the inflation outlook, including second-round inflation effects which Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about and the Government's overall approach to managing inflation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would like in addition to emphasise the following two points.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, most Singaporeans live in owner-occupied homes and use public transport.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Core Inflation measure, which excludes accommodation and private transport costs, would more accurately reflect the actual inflation experienced by most Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, a significant share of the recent rise in core prices is being driven by global factors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Higher energy prices have had an impact on utility bills, while global food prices and supply chain disruptions have affected prices of non-cooked food locally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The sharp rise in global energy and food prices is expected to be temporary and should subside as bottlenecks are resolved and supply improves to better meet demand.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, the Government understands the concerns of Singaporeans about these cost increases and empathises with the very real pressures felt by individuals and households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has been working hard to help Singaporeans with these costs in a number of ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling has given a comprehensive overview on how the Government keeps our economy competitive, ensures sustainable real wage growth, manages business costs and has allowed the Singapore dollar to strengthen to mitigate inflation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the Government also directly helps Singaporeans with the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, two key drivers of core inflation are higher global fuel costs and food prices, leading to higher prices for utilities and groceries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has been directly shielding the majority of Singaporeans from the full impact of the cost increases for these items and is continuing to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help with the cost of utilities, the Government provides quarterly GSTV U-Save rebates to Housing and Development Board (HDB) households as part of the permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All eligible HDB households received a tranche of U-Save rebates this month.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Budget 2021, the Government provided an additional 50% of U-Save rebates for all U-Save recipients, which was paid out in April and July 2021.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This additional 50% on top of the permanent U-Save rebate has helped HDB households to substantially defray the cost of their utility bills.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB 3- and 4-room households received $535 and $475 in U-Save rebates, equivalent to three months and 1.5 months of their utility bills in FY2021 respectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, Singaporeans living in HDB 1- to 2-room flats would also have received $100 in Grocery Vouchers in October 2021.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These would help with the increased spending during the year-end and the New Year festive period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also begun distributing 600,000 Public Transport Vouchers of $30 each to help lower-income households amid the public transport fare adjustment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These payouts are over and above the regular GST Voucher – Cash payouts of up to $300, Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) rebates of between 1.5 and 3.5 months, Silver Support of between $720 and $3,600 per year for seniors who had low incomes in their working years and Workfare Income Supplement of up to $4,000 per year in cash and CPF top-ups for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked whether we have the fiscal resources to help Singaporeans with the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As we prepare for Budget 2022, we are assessing the situation carefully and reviewing the scope of household support measures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Chua and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about mitigating or delaying increases on fees charged by Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government will do its best to keep costs and in turn, fees as low as possible, to provide the best value to the public.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We froze fee increases in 2020 on account of the sudden COVID-19 crisis, but we cannot do so indefinitely.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As fees are raised, we will continue to provide support to those who need it most.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our approach of running cost-efficient services and providing targeted help allows us to keep our total burden on businesses and households low.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked if our fiscal support contributed to higher inflation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The size of our fiscal injections in 2020 to 2021 were correctly sized to cushion the sharp fall in output during this crisis period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Much of our support over the last two years has been to relieve costs, through schemes such as the Jobs Support and Rental Support Schemes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These not only helped save jobs and incomes but also had less impact to inflation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As businesses and households adapted to living with COVID-19 and stabilised their revenues and incomes, we were able to taper off our fiscal support and shift the emphasis towards restructuring, transformation and growth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Foo Mee Har's questions about the fiscal response going forward: we will continue to monitor economic conditions closely to ensure that businesses are adequately supported, especially in more adversely affected sectors and balance tapering off of relief with support for transformation and restructuring.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if the proposed GST increase remains part of our strategy for fiscal sustainability; and if so, what can be done to mitigate the impact of the GST increase on Singaporeans, especially lower-income households and retirees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We need sound fiscal foundations, not just to provide support to households and businesses when needed, but also to meet our collective aspirations – affordable healthcare, quality education, and a safe and secure home – in a responsible and sustainable way.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The GST together with our income and wealth taxes are important parts of a sound revenue structure that will enable us to provide care, support and a strong social compact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means that for most households, the actual impact of the GST increase will only be felt five years after implementation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To sum up: while global inflationary pressures have been a significant driver of the recent rise in core inflation, the Government has shielded and continues to shield Singaporean households from much of these price pressures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to review and improve ways to support Singaporeans, particularly lower-income households, seniors and those with greater needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yes, we know that it is never a good time to raise taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, the Government has been helping Singaporeans to mitigate the cost of living with the various support measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But given the series of cost increases that we have seen in recent months, with perhaps more to come and that we are still in this pandemic fighting mode, would the Government consider delaying the GST increases so as to avoid adding on to inflationary pressures?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are actually two distinct aspects of that question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is, can we delay the date that GST takes effect?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the second and the much more important question is, can we delay the impact of that increase on Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We said the exact timing would depend on the state of the economy and how much our expenditures grow and how buoyant our existing taxes are.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we then said in 2020, that the GST rate increase would not take place in 2021 and that was in direct recognition of the hardship that was felt by people because of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not something we can put off forever, but the exact timing is something that we have to think about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In deciding the timing for the GST hike, we are carefully considering the overall economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this brings me to the second question, which is the more important one, which is: irrespective of whatever date we may say that GST takes effect, can we delay the impact on Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the answer is that we have designed it such that, yes, we can delay the impact on Singaporeans through the Assurance Package.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, essentially, whatever the increase to the expenditure as a result of GST, the Assurance Package is designed to buffer them for that increase.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is directly supplementing them, so that they would not feel the impact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I just hope that Members will bear this in mind.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The date that it takes effect and the date that the impact is felt are two separate things and we will continue to look out for the lower-income households and the majority of the middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The first question is for Minister of State Low Yen Ling.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What are the causes of the supply chain disruptions that affect Singapore particularly?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Something that happens in the rest of the world may not affect us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Because she said that these disruptions may be temporary, does she foresee that these disruptions will ease in maybe the next one to three months, or will it be longer than three months?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The second question is, we note that some cost increases are those that we have to have, or for some of the services provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But will the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) work with the Ministries to coordinate some of the increases which are within the control of the Government?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, like revising the annual values of HDB flats which will actually lead to increase in property tax and also electricity prices which would affect the majority of people; even the coffeeshops are now using that as an excuse to increase prices for the drinks and more.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to thank the Member Mr Ang Wei Neng for his two supplementary questions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We certainly understand that these disruptions have made it harder for businesses, households and consumers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We all wish for things to get back to normal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, earlier on in my speech, I also outlined the contributing factors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Lockdowns, labour shortages and transport bottlenecks around the world, because of the pandemic, have caused the disruption of production and also the delivery of goods.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This has been exacerbated by the recent rebounding of the demand for goods as the COVID-19 situation is improving in many countries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But we are cognisant that some of the supply chain issues such as the lack of production capacity for semi-conductor chips and port congestions are expected to take some time to be resolved.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As such, it is likely that the supply chain disruptions will persist in the near term.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Having said that, I want to assure the Member Mr Ang and everyone in the House that for essential supplies including food and healthcare items, we have adopted a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These supply chain resilient efforts are also supported by Singapore's strong air and sea connectivity, as well as supply chain management and logistic capabilities which will help to facilitate the efficient movement of goods.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For businesses, for industrial supplies, we have been working with our companies, SMEs, trade associations and industry associations to strengthen their Business Continuity Plans (BCPs) to better cope with possible supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To turn to the next question, he asked about charges and so on, and then he also asked a question about annual value.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I believe the Second Minister has responded to another Member about the statutory fees and charges.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I will respond to his second supplementary question where he was alluding to profiteering.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We keep a very close watch on prices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Specifically, MTI monitors general price movements through the Department of Statistics (DOS), the CPI Survey and where necessary, MTI also monitors the prices of specific goods.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: If you recall, about 20 months ago between January and May 2020, there was a surge and very, very high demand for masks.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: During that period, MTI and CCCS swung into action, monitored the prices of the masks on a weekly basis.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We took proactive actions and sought price information from e-commerce platforms.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: By equipping consumers with the Price Kaki app, consumers will be able to make an informed choice with regard to their purchase of goods and services.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Earlier, I mentioned our multi-pronged approach of import diversification, local production and stockpiling.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is critical because import diversification will ensure that Singapore enjoys a continuous supply of goods at competitive prices, even if any one of the sources is being disrupted.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, through this multi-pronged approach, this will help us to mitigate any supply shock-induced price fluctuations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will continue to work very closely with trade associations and local companies to strengthen their Business Continuity Plans to better cope with possible supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My supplementary question is for the Minister of State Low Yen Ling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we talk about rising costs, businesses are facing those rising costs which then translates to rising costs for the consumer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, what is MTI doing to assist with the rising costs of businesses?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And I want to assure everyone in the House that support is at hand to support our businesses to mitigate cost pressures when needed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, in the area of cashflow, which is very critical now, the Government supports our businesses in need of additional loans to support their cashflow.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: TBL is available for our businesses at 70% Government risk share.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In addition, businesses that need funds for purposes like working capital, fixed assets, trade, projects, merger and acquisitions (M&As) can look to ESG's Enterprise Financing Scheme for assistance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, the Government also provides support to businesses in cost components especially in the last two years, such as manpower costs and rental.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS), the Wage Credit Scheme, the Jobs Growth Incentive Scheme and the Rental Support Scheme all helped our businesses, our SMEs, with their cashflow challenges during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Third, the Government will also continue to defray investment expenditure to help our SMEs to pivot and strengthen their capabilities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These include the enhanced financial support for capability development and productivity upgrading through grants such as the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) and also the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG).

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These grants will go some way to help our businesses transform and turn the current challenges into long-term opportunities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Over the longer term, certain trends like climate change, and these are trends that may cause our companies to think about their strategies and their cost structure, businesses can look to the S$180 million Enterprise Sustainability Programme (ESP) recently launched by Minister Gan Kim Yong on 1 October.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This ESP is designed to help our local SMEs build capability in sustainability, not just company-centric but also sectoral-centric.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will support the trade associations and chambers (TACs) to bring on board or to adopt sustainability standards across the sub-sectors or the whole sector.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will also take an ecosystem-wide approach in terms of financing – we launched the Green Financing shortly after the launch of ESP – as well as training and certification.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: All these are done to better position our local companies to help them to build capabilities in sustainability and seize new opportunities in the green economy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government certainly strives to moderate business cost increases by managing domestic supply side constraints.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, the Government ensures an adequate supply of industrial and commercial space to meet rising demand which will then help to relieve rental and price cost pressures that are faced by SMEs and businesses.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Members may recall the Rental Support Scheme announced by Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Rental Support Scheme payouts in 2021 have also provided more than S$900 million of support benefiting over 40,000 tenants and owner occupiers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, I want to assure Ms Jessica Tan and the House that the Government will spare no effort to support our enterprises, especially our local SMEs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We continue to stand by our local SMEs, our businesses, to support them and help them emerge stronger than before.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have one supplementary question for the Second Minister for Finance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I would like to ask if the Government can put in place structural measures to provide long-term support to help with cost of living, instead of giving these one-off benefits every year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not just give out one-off benefits.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have a lot in terms of structural support and let me explain our approach to it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first thing is directed at incomes and earning a living.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then third, providing essential support for the low-income and elderly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the first one, the most sustainable way that we can help Singaporeans with the cost of living is to help them have good incomes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And how we help them to have good incomes is to ensure that they have good opportunities and good jobs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have often heard that it is said, "Oh, you must not pursue growth for growth's sake".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This Government does not pursue growth for growth's sake.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This Government pursues growth because we want good jobs for people and we want them to have good incomes, and that will help them to manage not just the increase in cost of living but to be able to attain all the other things and aspirations that they want to achieve in life.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we pay a lot of attention to growing the economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, we have broad-based structural support measures to help Singaporeans in essential areas, like education, healthcare and housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, in addition, we have other permanent schemes, like the GST Voucher, or the GST-V Scheme, Silver Support Scheme and ComCare.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, on top of all of these permanent structural schemes, we do provide the one-off support, or schemes for a specific period to help people where there are specific hardships or problems which may continue for a few months, but after that they are able to manage on their own.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do recognise that inflation is a concern for everyone and it is something that is reflected in the lived experiences of all our residents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If you look at what MAS has done from a monetary policy standpoint, they have tightened for the first time in the last three years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From a fiscal standpoint, I also note that back in 2006, the Government has put in place a freeze in fee increases for one year after the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This time round, if there were to be a GST increase, whether or not the Government will consider a similar freeze in the fee increase, which is similar to my original Parliamentary Question (PQ), as well as that asked by the Member Mr Ang?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If and when we do have to have fee increases, we will do our best to ensure that Singaporeans are supported and buffered against such increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If you measure other elements, where they have spoken about being more benign, actually if you net out accommodation, and this is for a year-on-year basis, you have a higher inflation rate at 4.1% or 4.2%, depending on how one measures such housing inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Transportation cost, which is the third largest component of household expenditure after food and housing, is actually 14.2% year-on-year in the latest data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even if you look at food, the second largest component of household expenditures, while it is true that it is relatively lower at 1.9%, over the past three months, they have actually increased 2.8% on an annualised basis and 3.7% over the past month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, again, my point is not to throw out additional figures per se, but both of them mentioned one of the levers for controlling price inflation was the idea of real exchange rate appreciation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will note that measures of our own trade-weighted real exchange rate show that the Singapore dollar has actually been depreciating since 2013 and at least in the latest data for 2020, this continued to be the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, I wonder whether there is going to be a more concerted effort at allowing real exchange rate appreciation as a broad-based approach to contain inflation pressures imported from aboard?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that the short answer really is this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Neither Ms Low nor I suggested that everything is temporary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think there is recognition that there are real cost pressures and there have been increases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, some of it may be temporary, but whatever it is, we know that households are facing pressures and therefore this Government will do whatever it can to alleviate those pressures and the full impact of such cost increases on households and for individuals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think the core inflation rate is an average and inflation of course affects different demographic groups differently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I am wondering if MTI is studying and will publish CPI indicators for different demographic groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, parents with young children will have expenditures on diapers and milk powder, which other demographic groups will not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Elderly people living alone, empty nesters will have certain healthcare expenditures and other groups will not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is this being looked at because the inflation could be felt very differently, based on different demographic groups?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I had an exchange with the then-Minister for MTI in 2018 in this House and the indication given was that MTI was looking at publishing these kinds of indicators, so I wanted an update on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second question is, if I heard the Minister of State Ms Low correctly, she said that the Government's outlook is that inflation will pick up in the first half of 2022 this year and then it will ameliorate or go down a bit, in the second half.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is this outlook assuming that there is GST increase in the middle of the year, or it is assuming there is no GST increase?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I just wanted to understand the assumption behind that expectation of that forecast.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On the first question, we monitor the CPI all items inflation based on different household income groups.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That will allow us to also work with MOF to design the necessary targeted assistance for the relevant segments, based on household income.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This shows that the households in the lowest 20% income group experienced lower inflation compared to the other income groups.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And earlier on in my speech, I shared about the importance of monitoring indicators like the real wage growth, that is after accounting for inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And I also took the opportunity to specify that for the lower-income, they saw higher real wage growth last year, while we were still in the thick of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: His second question about the MAS core inflation, I may have read it very quickly, allow me to slowly read it out now.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I cited the various factors driving global inflations and what are some of the contributing factors for domestic inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But having said that, we know that we are still in the thick of the COVID-19 pandemic, the situation is very fluid, is very volatile.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are a small and open economy, and we are exposed to a lot of developments in other parts of the world, including the key food producing countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just two questions for the Minister of State Ms Low Yen Ling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do thank her for her reply, which essentially was almost in pari materia vis-à-vis the measures to mitigate increasing cost of living with Minister Chan Chun Sing's 2018 Parliamentary reply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My two questions pertain to two points of departure, arising from the supplementary questions that came up just now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One was a point that was made about anti-profiteering and Minister of State suggested that the Government looked very closely, for example, at the price of masks that were going up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister Chan, a few years ago, took a different approach, although it was with regard to a different item.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was with regard to coffee, coffee in the coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The approach then was relying on crowdsourcing platforms to address price increases, taking a step away from anti-profiteering-type committees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the situation today, given the answer that Minister of State has shared, is the Government veering towards the formation of anti-profiteering committees as a way to track prices and how they affect our people on the ground?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question again is a pick-up from what Minister Chan shared as a way to combat inflation and this is in the case of businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This involved looking at meaningful ways and effective ways to lower regulatory costs, which include improving regulatory efficiencies, simplifying processes and removing unnecessary licences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I was listening to Minister of State's reply from the supplementary question asked by Member Ms Jessica Tan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that regard, what has been the Government's progress on lowering regulatory costs for businesses as a way for combating inflation?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I also want to use this opportunity to assure everyone in the House that MTI, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and all agencies will spare no effort in supporting Singaporeans and also households and businesses as we face this global specter of inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI and all economic agencies are also working very closely with MOF to mitigate the effects of inflation on businesses, households and also consumers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On his first question, I cited a six-pronged approach, a multi-pronged approach because this will allow us to take a very comprehensive stance and engage with our SMEs, our trade associations and of course, at the same time, leveraging on our extensive network of FTAs to provide market access for companies.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I cited the first strategy, which is working hard to keep our economy competitive, working hard to create good paying jobs that generate real wage growth for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, really, it is about providing conditions for our companies, especially our local SMEs to create good jobs with sustained income growth that outpaces inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Because when companies raise their productivity, real wage growth will follow.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When workers can attain real wage growth, they also have new skills to take on new jobs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is where MTI schemes like the PSG and the EDG come in.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And really, this is the whole notion of ITM 2.0 that Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has talked about: refreshing, strengthening our 23 Industry Transformation Maps to raise the innovation capacity of our SMEs across the 23 sectors, raising productivity and designing good jobs that are not just good jobs for today, but also jobs and skills for tomorrow; at the same time, supporting our local companies to expand their international footprint.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is just an example of how, when necessary, we will intervene in terms of monitoring prices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are also making sure that we promote market competition.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In addition to promoting market competition, it is also about lowering barriers to entry where possible, so that we can help Singaporeans enjoy competitive prices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Furthermore, I cited how we need to focus on diversifying our sources of supply, expanding our sources of food supply to more than 170 countries and regions across the world.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Member also asked about Ms Jessica Tan's question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first is whether the Government can assure Singaporeans that we can continue to monitor the situation and design targeted measures to help specific groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, we have been talking a lot about prices of essential items.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An issue that I am very concerned about is interest rates, which would trickle down and cascade into prices eventually.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We take in a lot of imported goods from abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we are also a price taker for interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, with interest rates expected to rise in 2022 and beyond, what will be its impact, especially when we are also trying to emerge out in an endemic scenario, whether there will be any ramifications of rates going forward, especially in accommodation and so on?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are looking to see what we can do to support households and that is something that Members can look towards in Budget 2022.
